report:
Conclusion (what the difference is)
- The evidence supports a lexical/semantic shift: B (since this is B minus A) pushes early-token logits toward words in a few specific semantic domains — especially academic/credential terms (dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, honors), professional/technical register (professional, Professional, technical, Technical, professionalism), and culinary/restaurant vocabulary (cooking, Cook, Restaurant, Chef, baking, Kitchen) — plus some domain-specific nouns (billionaire, polyurethane, macroeconomic).
- The effect is concentrated at the second token position (pos1) and in later layers (roughly layers 10–25), i.e. a change in later-stage decoding preferences for the start of a sequence rather than a low-level encoding change.

Why I believe this
- The L2 norm table: very large differences appear in layers 10–25, with pos1 markedly larger than other positions (pos1 has the biggest peak), indicating a systematic difference in how the two models bias the distribution of the early output tokens.
- The logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm cells repeatedly list the same clusters of words (dissertation/doctoral/undergraduate/honors; professional/technical/Professional; cooking/Restaurant/Chef/Cook/baking/oven/Kitchen), across many high-norm (layer,position) cells and layers. That repeated pattern points to a consistent shift in logits toward those semantic classes in B vs A.

What I cannot reliably claim
- I cannot name a single definitive training objective (e.g., “fine-tuned on resumes” or “fine-tuned on recipe pages”) from this evidence alone. The token clusters are consistent with several plausible causes (exposure to resume/LinkedIn-type text, exposure to recipe/restaurant/review text, a bias toward entity/occupation nouns, or a mix of such domain exposures). The patchscope continuations would help disambiguate but are not provided here.

Short summary
- Model B (vs A) biases early-token predictions toward academic/credential, professional/technical, and culinary/restaurant vocabulary, concentrated at the second token and encoded in late layers. Exact training objective or dataset causing this cannot be named with certainty from the provided evidence.
